findings.text: The opening paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and why it matters, all in a few sentences. This is the strongest part of the page.
findings.source: header, first lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The first section after the header is an error message. The lede says Athena records the models, the verdict and the cost of each step, so a broken demo of exactly that is the first evidence a newcomer sees. It weakens trust right away.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: Nearly the whole page studies a different project (firstmate): its states, its exit codes and 45 claims. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to work out that this detail is a sample of Athena's output, not something they need to understand.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions t1–t12, Claims c1–c45

findings.text: The page does say why the firstmate study is there. But studies seem to be a side feature: the lede says Athena's main job is turning a request into a commit. The page shows no example of that main flow, such as a request, its commit and its cost.
findings.source: header: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and complete: a repository link, prerequisites with versions, an install command and a first command, with a note on what it acts on. The header links straight to them, so a newcomer knows what to do.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: This link is aimed at the project owner and is unexplained, so a newcomer won't know whether it concerns them. It sits right next to the main call to action.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: These parts describe Athena's internal process and repository layout. To a first-time visitor they read as notes for the maintainers rather than information for readers.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..."; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data"

findings.text: Saying plainly when a term is undefined is honest, and it fits the page's careful approach. But several core terms are left unexplained, which makes the firstmate sections harder to follow.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." (also endpoint, heartbeat, wake, durable record)
